prompts.prompt: Our VP sent a one-liner: 'Clean up the billing service and also add usage-based pricing, ideally before Q1.' Nobody knows what 'clean up' means, and the billing service has thin test coverage. Before anyone starts, analyze this request and write the analysis to analysis.md: what kind of work it is, what's ambiguous, what's in and out of scope, and which specialist agents should handle it in what order. Do not ask me questions directly; put any questions you'd need answered in the file.
prompts.why_discriminating: The skill classifies intent into six types, checks for anti-patterns, and says never combine refactoring with feature work; Scope Creep also triggers intake questioning. Without it, a model tends to produce a single combined plan for 'clean up + pricing' and start sketching the pricing design.

floor_checks.text: Scope boundaries distinguish in scope from out of scope
floor_checks.check: grep -qi 'IN SCOPE' analysis.md && grep -qi 'OUT OF SCOPE' analysis.md

rubric.criterion: Flags the bundled refactor + new feature as a problem and splits them
rubric.pass: Names Scope Creep (and/or the do-not-combine-refactoring-with-features rule) and proposes separate tracks with the refactor gated on safety checks
rubric.partial: Notes the bundling but still plans them as one stream

rubric.pass: One of the six intent types per track (e.g. Refactoring for clean-up, Build from Scratch or Architecture for pricing) with a confidence level and rationale; confidence is not High given the ambiguity
rubric.partial: Type given but no confidence or rationale

rubric.criterion: Intake questions are concrete and placed in the file
rubric.pass: Specific questions on what 'clean up' means, the Q1 deadline's firmness, usage metrics to bill on, and pricing ownership, feeding Key Ambiguities

rubric.criterion: Recommended agent chain uses the framework's real specialist agents in a sensible order
rubric.pass: Ordered chain of existing k-* agents (k-product-manager, k-architect, k-developer, k-researcher) each with a purpose
rubric.partial: Sensible chain but invented or generic role names

rubric.pass: No pricing design, no invented facts about the billing service; IN/OUT/DEFERRED lists are explicit

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Would a team lead know how to split and staff this?
Are the ambiguities turned into answerable questions?
Does it avoid designing before scoping?

prompts.prompt: Request from the platform team: 'The data pipeline is slow, look into why and maybe redesign it.' It's a nightly Spark job feeding the finance warehouse. No numbers, no deadline. Do an upfront analysis before we commit anyone, and save it to analysis.md. No questions to me in chat; put them in the file.
prompts.why_discriminating: Under the skill this is Research: define exit criteria, set a time bound, and route to k-researcher before any architect, while flagging Analysis Paralysis/Premature Optimization. Without it, models jump to a redesign proposal or an open-ended investigation plan.

floor_checks.text: Scope boundaries distinguish in scope from out of scope
floor_checks.check: grep -qi 'IN SCOPE' analysis.md && grep -qi 'OUT OF SCOPE' analysis.md

rubric.criterion: Classified as Research (with Architecture only after findings), with rationale and confidence
rubric.pass: Research, rationale cites unknown root cause; redesign conditional on findings
rubric.partial: Architecture first, or Research without rationale

rubric.pass: Explicit exit criteria ('done when we know the top bottleneck stage and its share of runtime'), a time box, and an output format
Flags Premature Optimization ('maybe redesign' before measuring) and/or Analysis Paralysis, with the mitigation
k-researcher first, k-architect only if findings warrant; concrete questions (current runtime vs SLA, data volume trend, cost budget)

rubric.criterion: No speculative diagnosis presented as fact
rubric.partial: Some guesses stated as likely causes without labels

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Is the investigation bounded so it can finish?
Is the redesign deferred until there is evidence?
Are the questions ones the team can answer?

prompts.prompt: Ticket text: 'Restructure the order module into smaller services-style packages. Do not change behavior.' It's a Python monolith, about 40k lines, with decent test coverage and a nightly integration suite. Write a pre-implementation analysis to analysis.md covering intent, risks, scope, and who should do it. Don't ask questions.
prompts.why_discriminating: The skill's Refactoring branch carries specific safety directives (pre-refactor verification, verify after each change, documented preserved behavior, rollback, hidden dependencies) and routes to k-developer; it should not escalate to interactive elicitation for a clear, High-confidence refactor. Generic answers either miss the safety directives or over-ask.

rubric.pass: Pre-refactor baseline (tests green, behavior inventory), verify after each change, documented preserved behavior, and a rollback strategy
Hidden dependencies (circular imports, shared module state, DB session/transaction coupling, monkeypatched tests), propagation scope, import-path breakage for callers

rubric.criterion: Routes to k-developer with incremental slicing
rubric.pass: k-developer, one package extracted at a time behind compatibility re-exports
High (or Medium with reason) confidence, no unnecessary elicitation, explicitly excludes feature changes and lists DEFERRED work
rubric.partial: Asks questions already answered by the ticket
rubric.fail: Adds features or redesign to the scope

pairwise.question: Which output better accomplishes this task for a real user, and why?
focus: Would this keep the refactor from breaking production?
Are the risks specific to splitting a Python monolith?
Is the analysis proportionate to a clear ticket?
